lessons.title: Control where links open and what they point at
lessons.summary: Master the target attribute, safe new-tab links with rel="noopener", in-page fragment links, and special schemes like mailto:, tel: and downloadable files.
lessons.goal: Build a contact page whose links open in the right place, jump to the right section, and trigger email, phone and download actions.
lessons.whyItMatters: A link is more than a blue underline: the target attribute decides whether it replaces the current page or opens a new tab, and getting that wrong frustrates users or leaks a security hole. Fragment links power every 'back to top' button and table of contents on the web. mailto:, tel: and download links turn a static page into something people can act on with one tap.

After this lesson the same page has a portfolio link that opens in a fresh tab (so the visitor never loses the photographer's page), a jump link straight to the contact section, a one-click email link, and a price list that downloads instead of opening.

commonMistakes: Writing target="blank" without the underscore. That is not a keyword — it creates a named window called 'blank', which behaves confusingly on repeat clicks.
Using target="_blank" without rel="noopener". Older browsers give the new page a window.opener reference it can abuse to redirect your page.
Linking to href="#contact" but forgetting to put id="contact" on any element. The click then does nothing (or jumps to the top).
Adding a space in mailto: links, such as mailto: name@example.com. The scheme must run straight into the address with no space.
lessons.proTip: Modern browsers treat target="_blank" as if rel="noopener" were present, but write it explicitly anyway: it documents your intent, protects visitors on older browsers, and satisfies security linters that flag the bare form.

sections.heading: The target attribute: where a link opens
sections.body:
By default, clicking a link replaces the current page. That default has a name: target="_self". You almost never write it, because it is what happens anyway, but knowing it exists makes the other values easier to understand.

The value you will actually use is target="_blank", which opens the destination in a new tab (or a new window, depending on the visitor's browser settings). It is the right choice when the visitor is in the middle of something on your page — filling a form, reading an article — and the link leads somewhere external they will want to glance at and come back from.

The underscore matters. _blank, _self, _parent and _top are reserved keywords; any other string is treated as a window name. target="blank" (no underscore) opens a window named 'blank' and then reuses that same window for every later click, which is rarely what anyone intends.

sections.heading: _parent and _top: the frame escape hatches
sections.body:
Two more keywords exist for pages embedded inside other pages with frames or iframes. target="_parent" loads the destination in the parent document — the page one level up from the frame the link lives in. target="_top" goes further and loads it in the full browser tab, breaking out of every level of nesting at once.

If your page is not inside a frame, both behave exactly like _self, so they are harmless but pointless. You will meet them mostly in embedded widgets, ad units, and older framed sites. Recognize them when you read code; reach for them only when you are genuinely working inside an iframe.

sections.heading: Why _blank needs rel="noopener"
sections.body:
When a link opens a new tab, the new page historically received a JavaScript reference back to yours, called window.opener. A malicious destination could use it to quietly redirect your original tab to a look-alike phishing page — an attack known as tabnabbing. The visitor switches back to what they think is your site and types their password into a fake.

Adding rel="noopener" severs that reference: the new tab gets no handle on the old one. A related value, rel="noreferrer", additionally stops the browser from telling the destination which page the visitor came from; you can combine them as rel="noopener noreferrer".

Current browsers now apply noopener behavior to every target="_blank" link automatically, but explicit is better than implied: it keeps older browsers safe and makes the security decision visible in your source.

sections.heading: Fragment links: jumping inside a page
sections.body:
An href that starts with # does not fetch anything — it scrolls. href="#contact" tells the browser to find the element whose id is contact on the current page and bring it into view. The pair is always the same: a link with #some-id, and exactly one element somewhere on the page carrying id="some-id".

This is the mechanism behind tables of contents, 'skip to content' accessibility links, and every 'back to top' button. For back-to-top you give an element near the top an id (the h1 is a common host) and link to it from the bottom. A bare href="#" also scrolls to the top, but it puts a stray # in the address bar and is often abused as a do-nothing placeholder, so prefer a real id.

The id value is case-sensitive and must be unique on the page — if two elements share it, the browser jumps to the first and the duplicate is a bug waiting to confuse someone.

sections.heading: Fragments on other pages
sections.body:
A fragment can ride along on any URL, not just the current page. href="pricing.html#enterprise" first loads pricing.html, then scrolls it to the element with id="enterprise". The same works with full external URLs: https://example.com/docs#installation.

This is how deep links into documentation work, and why well-chosen ids on your headings are a gift to anyone who wants to share a precise spot on your page. The fragment lives after the # in the address bar and never gets sent to the server — the server returns the whole page and the browser does the scrolling on its own.

sections.heading: Links that are not pages: mailto: and tel:
sections.body:
The href attribute accepts more schemes than http and https. href="mailto:nadia@example.com" opens the visitor's default mail program with the To field pre-filled. You can pre-fill more by appending URL parameters: mailto:nadia@example.com?subject=Booking adds a subject line.

href="tel:+302101234567" dials a number — on phones it opens the dialer, and on desktops it may hand off to a calling app. Always write the number in international form with a leading + and no spaces or dashes inside the href; format the visible link text however reads best.

One caveat for mailto: it only works if the visitor has a mail client configured, which is not guaranteed on shared or public computers. Show the address as the visible text too, so it can be copied by hand as a fallback.
sections.code: nadia@example.com +30 210 123 4567

sections.heading: The download attribute
sections.body:
By default a browser displays whatever it can — PDFs, images, text files all open in the tab. Adding the download attribute to a link flips that behavior: the browser saves the file instead of navigating to it.

The attribute can stand alone (<a href="price-list.pdf" download>) or carry a value that suggests a filename for the saved copy: download="nadia-prices-2026.pdf". The value only renames the download; the href still decides what is fetched.

One important restriction: browsers honor the download attribute only for files from your own origin (your own site). For cross-origin URLs it is ignored and the link navigates normally — a deliberate safety rule so pages cannot force-download files from other sites under misleading names.

lessons.title: Put images on a page the right way
lessons.summary: Use img with src and meaningful alt text, reserve space with width and height, pick the right file format, and make images clickable.
lessons.goal: Build a small photo page with a properly described main image, a decorative divider, dimension attributes that prevent layout shift, and a clickable thumbnail.
lessons.whyItMatters: Images carry most of a page's visual weight and most of its download size, so small markup decisions have outsized effects. Good alt text is the difference between a blind visitor understanding your page and hitting a dead end, and it is what search engines index. Width and height attributes stop the page from jumping around while photos load — one of the metrics Google actually scores sites on.
steps: Read how img, src and alt work together.
Add the main harbour photo with its src (task 1).
Write descriptive alt text for it (task 2), using the alt-writing section as a guide.
Add width and height so the browser can reserve space (task 3).
Read the decorative-image section, then add the divider with an empty alt (task 4).
Wrap the thumbnail in a link to make it clickable (task 5), then Run.
lessons.explanation: The first img names its file in src, describes its content in alt for anyone who cannot see it, and declares its dimensions so the browser reserves the right amount of space before the file arrives. The second image is pure decoration, so its alt is deliberately empty — screen readers skip it entirely instead of announcing a useless filename. The third img sits inside an <a>, which makes the whole picture clickable; its alt then describes where the link goes.
lessons.example: A photo diary page written carelessly: — no alt, no dimensions. A screen-reader user hears 'IMG 4021 jpeg', the page reflows twice while images load, and Google has no idea what the photo shows. The corrected page describes each meaningful photo in a short sentence, silences the decorative divider with alt="", declares every image's width and height, and loads instantly into a stable layout.
lessons.exercise: In the editor on the right, complete a harbour photo diary: add the main photo with src, descriptive alt, and width/height; add a decorative divider with an empty alt; and wrap the gallery thumbnail in a link.
lessons.expectedResult: The preview shows the page structure with image placeholders in stable, correctly sized boxes (the sample files do not exist, which is fine — the checks read your markup, not the pixels). All five checks pass.
commonMistakes: Omitting alt entirely. Screen readers then fall back to reading the filename, and validators flag the page. Every img needs an alt attribute — even if its value is empty.
Writing alt text that starts with 'image of' or 'picture of'. The screen reader already announces it as an image; describe the content itself.
Giving decorative images real alt text. A flourish or divider described aloud is noise; use alt="" so assistive tech skips it.
Leaving out width and height 'because CSS will size it anyway'. Without them the browser cannot reserve space, and the page jumps as each image arrives.
lessons.proTip: A quick alt-text test: imagine reading the page aloud over the phone to someone. Whatever you would naturally say when you reach the picture — that is the alt text. If you would say nothing and keep reading, the image is decorative and gets alt="".

sections.heading: The img element: src is the picture
sections.body:
Images arrive on a page through the img element. It is a void element — no closing tag, no content of its own — because the content is the file named in its src attribute. The browser reads src, fetches that file as a separate download, and paints it where the img sits in the document.

The src value is a URL like any link target: a filename in the same folder (harbour.jpg), a path (images/harbour.jpg), or a full address on another server. If the file cannot be fetched, the browser shows a broken-image icon plus the alt text — which is your first hint of why alt matters so much.

Because every image is an extra download, each one has a cost. A page with ten photos makes ten additional requests, and the total file size directly controls how long a visitor on a slow connection waits.

sections.heading: Writing alt text that actually helps
sections.body:
The alt attribute holds the text that replaces the image when the image cannot be seen: for blind visitors using screen readers, for anyone whose connection failed mid-load, and for search engines, which cannot see pixels at all.

Good alt text answers one question: what would the visitor miss if the image vanished? Describe the content and its point, briefly — 'Fishing boats moored in a harbour at sunrise' — not the medium ('a photo showing...') and not keywords stuffed for SEO. Aim for a phrase or short sentence; if an image needs a paragraph of explanation, that explanation belongs in the visible page text.

Context changes the right answer. The same chart could have alt="Sales rose 40% from January to June" on a results page, but alt="Example of a misleading truncated y-axis" in a design article. Write for what the image does on this page, not what it objectively is.

sections.heading: Decorative images: the empty alt
sections.body:
Not every image carries meaning. Dividers, background flourishes, and purely visual spacers add nothing a listener needs to know. For those, write alt="" — the attribute present, its value empty.

The distinction matters: an empty alt tells screen readers 'skip this, it is decoration', while a missing alt attribute tells them 'the author forgot', and most will read the filename aloud as a guess. So the rule is absolute: every img gets an alt attribute; the only choice is whether its value describes the image or is deliberately empty.

When in doubt, ask whether the page loses information if the image disappears. Loses information: describe it. Loses only prettiness: alt="".

sections.heading: width, height and layout shift
sections.body:
Until an image file arrives, the browser has no idea how big it is — so by default it renders the page without reserving space, then shoves everything downward when the image finally loads. That jump is called layout shift, and it is genuinely hostile: visitors tap the wrong button because the page moved under their finger. Google measures it as Cumulative Layout Shift and ranks pages on it.

The fix costs two attributes: width and height, in pixels, matching the image file's real proportions. The browser uses their ratio to reserve a correctly shaped box immediately, and the image loads into a space that was always there. CSS can still scale the displayed size later; the attributes' job is the placeholder ratio, not the final look.

Write them as bare numbers — width="640", not width="640px". The px is implied in HTML attributes; the unit syntax belongs to CSS.

sections.heading: Choosing a file format
sections.body:
Six formats cover practically every image on the web, and each has a natural home. JPG (or JPEG) compresses photographs well by discarding detail your eye barely notices; it is the default for photos but blurs sharp-edged graphics. PNG is lossless and supports transparency, which makes it right for screenshots, logos with transparent backgrounds, and any graphic with crisp lines — at the price of larger files for photos.

GIF is the legacy option: only 256 colors, but it animates, which kept it alive for memes; for everything else it has been superseded. SVG is not pixels at all but geometry — a text file of shapes that scales to any size without blurring, perfect for icons, logos and diagrams, and usually tiny.

WebP and AVIF are the modern generation: they compress both photos and graphics substantially better than JPG and PNG, support transparency and animation, and are now supported by all current browsers. For new work, WebP is a safe default for photographic content, with AVIF squeezing files even smaller where the encoder is available. The practical rule: photos in WebP or JPG, sharp graphics in SVG or PNG, and animation in video formats rather than GIF when you can.

sections.heading: Images as links, and title vs alt
sections.body:
Wrap an img in an <a> and the entire picture becomes clickable — the standard pattern for logos that link home and thumbnails that open galleries. When an image is a link, its alt text should describe the destination or action ('Open the full harbour gallery'), because for a screen-reader user that alt is the link text.

The title attribute is a different, weaker tool: it produces the small tooltip that appears when a mouse hovers. It is not a substitute for alt — touchscreen users never see tooltips, and screen readers do not reliably read them. Use title, sparingly, for a bonus hint on top of solid alt text, never instead of it.

lessons.title: Caption images with figure and give your site a favicon
lessons.summary: Use figure and figcaption to bind images to their captions, sketch a clickable image map with map and area, and add the little tab icon every real site has.
lessons.goal: Publish a chart page with a semantically captioned figure, a clickable region on a floor plan, and a favicon in the head.
lessons.whyItMatters: A caption sitting in a loose paragraph under an image is only visually attached; figure and figcaption attach it structurally, so screen readers, search engines and reader modes know the two belong together. And the favicon is often the first detail visitors judge: a site without one looks unfinished in every browser tab, bookmark list and history entry.

lessons.explanation: The figure element declares 'this image and this caption are one unit that could be moved elsewhere without breaking the text around it'. The figcaption inside it is the caption — machines now know exactly which text describes which image. The link rel="icon" in the head points the browser at the small image it shows in the tab, in bookmarks, and in history; sizes and type help it pick the right file when several are offered.
lessons.example:
A report page shows a chart with the caption in a plain

below it. Visually fine — but a screen reader reads them as two unrelated blocks, and a reader mode may keep the image and drop the caption. Wrapped in figure/figcaption, the pair travels together everywhere: assistive tech announces the caption as belonging to the chart, and the browser tab now shows the company's little icon instead of a generic gray globe.

commonMistakes: Placing figcaption outside the figure. It must be a child of figure — first or last inside it — or it is just a stray element.
Using figcaption as a replacement for alt. They serve different readers: alt describes the image for those who cannot see it; the caption adds context for everyone.
Forgetting that usemap's value needs the # prefix (usemap="#plan") while the map's name has none (name="plan").
Linking the favicon from a subpage-relative path so it breaks on nested pages. Use a root-relative path like /favicon.png on real sites.
lessons.proTip: Browsers request /favicon.ico from your site root automatically even with no link tag — dropping a favicon.ico there is a zero-markup fallback that also covers old bookmarks. A modern setup pairs it with an SVG icon: <link rel="icon" href="/icon.svg" type="image/svg+xml">.

sections.heading: figure: content that stands apart
sections.body:
Some content is referenced by the text rather than woven into it: a chart, a photo, a code listing, a quoted poem. HTML marks that kind of content with the figure element. The definition to remember: a figure is self-contained — you could move it to the bottom of the page or into an appendix, and the surrounding paragraphs would still read correctly.

That test tells you when figure is right. 'As figure 1 shows, sales rose steadily' — the chart can float anywhere, so it is a figure. An icon inside a sentence cannot move without breaking the sentence, so it is not.

A figure is not limited to one image: it can hold several images sharing one caption, a code snippet, a table, a video — any self-contained block that deserves a label.

sections.heading: figcaption: the caption that machines can see
sections.body:
Inside a figure you may place exactly one figcaption, either as the first child or the last — caption above or caption below, your choice. Its text is the figure's label, and because the relationship is structural rather than visual, every consumer of the page gets it: screen readers announce the caption with the figure, search engines index them together, and reader modes keep them paired.

figcaption complements alt; it never replaces it. The alt attribute serves someone who cannot see the image at all and describes its content. The caption serves everyone and adds context — the source, the date range, the 'Figure 1' number. A chart typically needs both: alt="Bar chart of monthly sales rising from January to June" and a caption of 'Figure 1: Monthly sales, Jan–Jun'.

sections.heading: Image maps: clickable regions with map and area
sections.body:
Occasionally one image needs several clickable zones — a floor plan where each room links to its own page, or a world map with per-country links. HTML's classic answer is the image map: the img gets a usemap attribute pointing at a named map element, and the map contains area elements, each defining one clickable shape.

Each area sets a shape (rect, circle or poly), coords giving the shape's pixel coordinates on the image, an href for the destination, and an alt describing the region — areas are links, so they need link text for assistive tech. The naming convention trips people up: the map declares name="plan" without a hash, while the image references it as usemap="#plan" with one.

Image maps are worth recognizing more than mastering: the pixel coordinates do not adapt when the image scales responsively, so modern sites usually reach for SVG or positioned links instead. But for a fixed-size diagram they still work in every browser.

sections.heading: The favicon: your site's smallest asset
sections.body:
The favicon (favorites icon) is the small image browsers display beside your page title — in the tab, in bookmarks, in the history list, and on some platforms in search results. It is declared in the head with a link element: rel="icon" plus an href to the image file.

The optional sizes attribute tells the browser what pixel dimensions a file provides (sizes="32x32"), and type names its MIME type (type="image/png"). You can list several link elements at different sizes and let the browser choose the best fit for each context — tabs want tiny icons, while a bookmark on a phone home screen wants a large one.

Even without any markup, browsers try one guess: they request a file called favicon.ico from the root of your site. That legacy behavior is why favicon.ico still exists on most servers, and why placing one there is a sensible safety net alongside your explicit links.
sections.code: <link rel="icon" href="favicon.png" sizes="32x32" type="image/png">

sections.heading: Favicon formats in practice
sections.body:
The traditional format is ICO — a container that bundles multiple sizes (16x16, 32x32, 48x48) in one file, which is exactly what favicon.ico is. PNG works in all modern browsers and is easier to produce; supply at least a 32x32, and a 180x180 or larger if you care about phone home screens.

SVG is the modern favorite where supported: one vector file stays sharp at any size and can even adapt to dark mode with embedded CSS. A robust minimal setup for a new site is two lines — an SVG icon for modern browsers and a favicon.ico fallback at the site root for everything else.

One practical note: browsers cache favicons aggressively. If you swap the icon and the tab keeps showing the old one, it is almost never your markup — force-refresh or bump the filename.

lessons.title: Organize anything with ordered and unordered lists
lessons.summary: Use ul, ol and li to structure bullet points, numbered steps and navigation menus — including nesting, the start and reversed attributes, and continuing numbers across lists.
lessons.goal: Build a trip-planner page with a bulleted packing list, numbered itinerary steps that continue across sections, a nested sub-list, and a list-based navigation menu.
lessons.whyItMatters: Lists are everywhere once you look: navigation menus, search results, step-by-step instructions, shopping carts. Marking them up as real ul/ol lists — instead of paragraphs with dashes — tells screen readers how many items there are and lets users jump between them, gives CSS a clean structure to style, and keeps numbered steps renumbering themselves automatically when you edit.
steps: Read what separates ordered from unordered lists.
Build the packing list as a ul with at least three items (task 1).
Build Saturday's itinerary as an ol (task 2).
Read about the start and reversed attributes, then make Sunday's list continue at 4 (task 3).
Nest a toiletries sub-list inside the packing list (task 4).
Read the navigation section and convert the top links into a nav menu (task 5), then Run.
lessons.explanation: The ul renders bullets because item order carries no meaning; the browser numbers the ol automatically, and start="4" makes its numbering continue from a previous list. The nested ul lives inside an li of its parent — a list is nested inside an item, never directly inside another list. Every visible entry, including the one hosting the sub-list, is an li.

As real lists, the packing items become scannable bullets, the itinerary numbers itself (and renumbers when a step is inserted), and the toiletries expand into an indented sub-list without touching anything else.

commonMistakes: Putting text or other elements directly inside ul or ol. The only valid children of a list are li elements — everything else goes inside an li.
Nesting a sub-list as a sibling of the li instead of inside it. The inner <ul> must sit within the parent <li>, before its closing tag.
Faking numbered lists by typing '1.', '2.' into paragraphs. The numbers stop matching reality the first time you insert a step.
Choosing ol just because numbers look tidier. If reordering the items would not change their meaning, the list is unordered.
lessons.proTip: Nearly every horizontal navigation bar on the web is secretly a ul — CSS removes the bullets and lines the items up. Keep the markup a real list even when it will not look like one: screen readers announce 'list, five items', which is exactly what a menu is.

coding.intro: You will structure a weekend-trip planner with every list pattern that matters: bullets, numbers, continued numbering, nesting, and a nav menu.

sections.heading: Two list types, one question
sections.body:
HTML offers two general-purpose list containers. ul (unordered list) renders its items with bullets; ol (ordered list) renders them with automatic numbers. Both hold the same kind of children: li (list item) elements, and nothing else directly — no loose text, no stray paragraphs between items.

The choice between them comes down to one question: does the order carry meaning? Steps in a recipe, ranked results, an itinerary — reorder those and the content breaks, so they are ordered. A packing list, a set of features, links in a menu — any order works, so they are unordered. The visual difference (bullets versus numbers) is just the symptom; the real distinction is semantic, and screen readers announce it.

Browsers indent both list types and pick the marker automatically. Each additional item is one more <li>, and the numbering of an ol maintains itself: insert a step in the middle and every number below it updates for free.

sections.heading: Tuning ordered lists: type, start, reversed
sections.body:
Ordered lists take three attributes worth knowing. type changes the numbering style: "1" for decimal (the default), "A" and "a" for letters, "I" and "i" for Roman numerals. Legal documents and outlines use the letter and Roman styles; most pages never need them.

start sets the first number: <ol start="4"> begins at 4. Its everyday use is continuing a sequence that was interrupted — steps 1-3 under one heading, then the list resumes at 4 under the next. The value is always a number even when type shows letters (start="3" with type="A" begins at C).

reversed is a boolean attribute that counts down instead of up — a top-ten list running 10 to 1 is <ol reversed>. It needs no value; its presence flips the direction. All three attributes belong on the ol itself, not on individual items.

sections.heading: Nesting lists inside lists
sections.body: Lists nest to any depth, and the rule for doing it correctly is strict: the inner list goes inside an li of the outer list — after that item's text, before its closing . The sub-list belongs to that item; putting it directly between two li elements is invalid and renders unpredictably. Browsers indent each level further and, for unordered lists, usually switch the bullet style per level (disc, then circle, then square), which gives free visual hierarchy. You can mix types freely: an ol of steps where one step contains a ul of options is perfectly normal. When nesting goes wrong it is almost always a closing-tag problem, so indent nested lists in your source exactly as you want to think about them — the inner ul visibly inside its host li.

    • Sunscreen

sections.heading: Lists as navigation menus
sections.body:
A navigation menu is, structurally, a list of links — and that is exactly how the web marks it up: a nav element wrapping a ul, each li containing one a. The nav element tells assistive technology 'this block is site navigation', and the list tells it how many destinations there are and lets users skip past them with one keystroke.

The pattern looks over-engineered until you see what each layer buys: nav gives the block a landmark role, ul/li gives it countable structure, and the anchors do the linking. CSS then removes the bullets and lays the items out horizontally — the markup stays a list even when it looks like a toolbar.

This is the single most common list you will ever write. Practically every site header on the web contains one.

  • Itinerary

sections.heading: What lists do not control: their looks
sections.body:
Everything visual about a list — the bullet symbol, custom markers, horizontal layout, indentation — belongs to CSS, chiefly the list-style family of properties. list-style-type swaps the marker (square, decimal, none), list-style-image replaces it with an image, and list-style: none removes markers entirely, which is step one of turning a list into a menu bar.

Older HTML had presentational attributes for some of this, and you will still meet type on ul in ancient code; treat it as historical. The division of labor is the same one running through this whole course: HTML says what the content is (a list, ordered or not), CSS says how it looks. Choose ul versus ol for meaning, then restyle freely.

lessons.summary: Use dl, dt and dd to mark up glossaries, FAQs and metadata — including several descriptions per term and richer markup inside definitions.
lessons.goal: Build a small web glossary as a dl, with one term carrying two descriptions and code markup nested inside a definition.
lessons.whyItMatters: Plenty of real content is name-value pairs: glossary terms and meanings, product specs and values, questions and answers. Bullet lists flatten those pairs into indistinguishable lines; the description list keeps the pairing explicit, so the structure survives into styling, screen readers and scripts. Once you can spot term-plus-description content, you will find uses for dl on nearly every project.

lessons.explanation: The dl is the container, each dt names a term, and every dd immediately following a dt describes it — so HTTP here owns two descriptions simply because two dd elements follow it. Definitions are ordinary flow content, which is why the HTML entry can nest a code element (and could nest paragraphs, links or lists). Browsers indent the dd elements by default, visually hanging each description under its term.
lessons.example:
A glossary drafted as bullets reads: 'HTML - the markup language', 'CSS - the stylesheet language'. The dash is doing structural work that only sighted readers can see.

Rebuilt as a dl, each term is a dt and each meaning a dd: screen readers announce term and description as a pair, CSS can style terms bold and definitions indented with two selectors, and adding a second meaning to a term is just one more dd.

commonMistakes: Writing definition text directly inside the dl. Only dt and dd (and wrapper div elements) may be children of dl — all prose lives in dd.
Pairing terms and definitions by proximity in a ul instead of using dl. The pairing then exists only visually and is lost to assistive tech.
Assuming one dt can have only one dd. Any number of dd elements may follow a term — and several dt elements may share one dd.
Using dl for content that is not name-value shaped, just to get indentation. Indentation is a CSS job; dl is for genuine term-description pairs.
lessons.proTip: dl is quietly ideal for metadata blocks: 'Author: N. Kim, Published: May 2026, Reading time: 6 min' is three dt/dd pairs. Many documentation sites render function parameters exactly this way — parameter name as dt, explanation as dd.

sections.heading: The third list type: dl, dt, dd
sections.body:
Beyond bulleted and numbered lists, HTML has a list built for pairs: the description list. Three elements share the work. dl (description list) is the container. dt (description term) holds a name — a word being defined, a spec label, a question. dd (description details) holds whatever describes the dt before it.

The pairing is positional: a dd belongs to the nearest dt above it. Browsers render dt elements flush left and indent each dd beneath its term, which is why glossaries built with dl look right with zero CSS.

Only dt and dd may appear directly inside a dl (a div wrapper around groups is also allowed, mainly for styling). Loose text between them is invalid — every piece of prose belongs inside a dd.
sections.code:
<dl>
  <dt>CSS</dt>
  <dd>The stylesheet language that controls how pages look.</dd>
</dl>

sections.heading: Several descriptions, several terms
sections.body:
The dt/dd relationship is not one-to-one. A term can be followed by multiple dd elements, each an additional description: a word with two senses, a spec with a value plus a footnote, a question with a short answer and a longer elaboration. All the dd elements between one dt and the next belong to that dt.

The reverse also works: several consecutive dt elements can share the dd that follows them — useful when two spellings or synonyms carry one definition ('colour', 'color', then a single dd).

This flexibility is exactly what ul and ol lack, and it is the reason dl exists: the grouping of names and values is expressed in the markup itself rather than implied by line breaks.
sections.code:
<dl>
  <dt>HTTP</dt>
  <dd>The protocol browsers use to request pages.</dd>
  <dd>Also the scheme at the front of most URLs.</dd>

  <dt>colour</dt>
  <dt>color</dt>
  <dd>Two spellings, one CSS property.</dd>
</dl>

sections.heading: Where description lists shine
sections.body:
Three content shapes come up constantly and all fit dl naturally. Glossaries and dictionaries are the textbook case: term, meaning. Metadata panels are the workhorse case: 'Author', 'Published', 'License' as dt elements with their values as dd — product spec sheets, recipe info boxes and API parameter tables are all this shape. And FAQs fit too: each question a dt, its answer a dd.

The test for whether dl is right: can you read the content aloud as 'X: Y' pairs without forcing it? 'HTML: the markup language' — natural, use dl. 'Rain jacket: ...' has no second half — that is a plain ul.

What dl is not for is layout. Early web developers used it to get indentation for free; today that is simply a styling decision made in CSS, and misusing dl for it confuses every machine reader of the page.

sections.heading: dl versus ul and ol
sections.body:
All three lists group items, so the differences are worth stating plainly. ul groups equal items whose order is free. ol groups equal items whose order is meaningful. dl groups unequal items — pairs in which one side names and the other side describes.

Structurally, ul and ol allow exactly one kind of child (li), while dl alternates two kinds (dt and dd) whose sequence encodes the pairing. That is also why you cannot get dl's semantics by styling a ul: the bullet list has no way to say which line defines which.

Screen readers reflect the distinction: a ul is announced as 'list, N items', while dl support varies but generally conveys term-description grouping. Choose by meaning and the announcement takes care of itself.

sections.heading: Rich content inside dd
sections.body:
A dd is not restricted to plain text — it accepts nearly any markup: paragraphs, links, emphasis, code, even entire nested lists. A glossary definition can therefore include a code example, an FAQ answer can contain a link to documentation, and a spec value can hold a small ul of options.

The dt is more constrained: it takes phrasing-level content (text, code, abbr and similar), not block structures like paragraphs or lists. Keep terms short and put anything substantial in the dd.

One pattern you will use in this exercise: writing about HTML inside HTML. To show a literal tag such as <h1> as text, its angle brackets must be written as the entities < and >, usually wrapped in a code element for monospace rendering — a preview of the entities lesson coming later in this course.

lessons.whyItMatters: Every layout question starts here: block elements stack vertically and claim the full width; inline elements flow inside lines of text. lessons.explanation: The div is a block: it starts on a new line, spans the available width, and groups the heading and paragraph into one styleable unit. The span is inline: it wraps two words mid-sentence without breaking the line, giving CSS and JavaScript a handle on just that phrase. Neither element means anything by itself — they exist purely to carry classes, ids and styles when no semantic element fits.

sections.heading: Two ways to occupy a page
sections.body:
Every visible HTML element renders in one of two basic modes. Block-level elements behave like stacked boxes: each one starts on a new line, stretches across the full available width, and pushes whatever follows below it. Inline elements behave like words: they sit inside a line of text, take only the width of their content, and wrap across lines exactly as words do. You have been using both all along. Headings, paragraphs and lists stack — block. Links, bold and italic sit mid-sentence — inline. The distinction explains rendering you may have wondered about: why two

elements never sit side by side, and why an never forces a line break. Keep one refinement in mind: 'block' and 'inline' describe default display behavior, not a permanent property. CSS's display property can make any element render either way. The HTML-level question is about defaults and about what is allowed to nest where.
sections.code:
Paragraphs stack on top of each other.

Like this — always a new line.

But links, bold and italics flow inside the sentence.

sections.heading: The block roster and the inline roster
sections.body:
The block-level elements you will use constantly: p, h1 through h6, div, ul, ol, li, dl, dt, dd, table, form, blockquote, pre, hr, and the semantic sections (header, footer, nav, main, section, article, aside, figure). Each claims its own horizontal band of the page.

The everyday inline elements: a, span, strong, b, em, i, small, mark, sub, sup, u, del, ins, code, abbr, br, img, input, button, label. They ride along inside lines. A couple are special: img and input are inline yet have intrinsic size, so they behave like an oversized character sitting on the text line — which is why images align with text baselines by default.

You do not need to memorize these lists; you need the instinct. Ask: does this element structure the page (block) or annotate text within a line (inline)? The instinct is right far more often than not, and the exceptions are learned by meeting them.

sections.heading: div: the generic block container
sections.body:
div is a block element with no meaning whatsoever. It says nothing about its content — it exists solely to group things, so that the group can be styled with CSS, targeted by JavaScript, or laid out as a unit. Wrap a heading and its paragraphs in <div class="card"> and you can border, shade and position them as one card.

Because it is meaningless, div is the tool of last resort, not first: if the group is navigation, use nav; if it is a standalone article, use article; if it is an image with a caption, use figure. Those elements group and carry meaning. Reach for div when no semantic element describes the group — which, in real layouts, is still remarkably often.

Divs nest freely inside other divs, and complex layouts are built from exactly such nesting. The discipline is to add wrappers when they earn their place, and to name them honestly with classes.

Remote, full time.

sections.heading: span: the generic inline container
sections.body: span is div's inline twin: a meaningless wrapper for a run of text within a line. It changes nothing visually on its own — its entire purpose is to give a phrase an identity that CSS or JavaScript can grab: New can be colored, badged or read by a script without disturbing the sentence it lives in. As with div, prefer meaning when meaning exists: emphasis is , importance is , highlighted relevance is , code is . span is for purely presentational or scripting hooks — highlighting a search match, styling the first word of a paragraph, wrapping a price so a script can update it. A span may contain other inline elements (a span holding a link is fine) but never block elements — a rule the next section makes precise.
sections.code: New this week: both roles above.

sections.heading: The nesting rules browsers enforce
sections.body:
Two rules govern who may contain whom. First: inline elements may contain other inline content, but never block elements. A div inside a span is invalid; so is a paragraph inside a link's text... with the modern exception that is allowed to wrap block content — the one inline element granted that power, which is how whole cards become clickable. Second, and the source of endless beginner confusion: the p element may contain only inline content. No div, no list, no table, not even another p inside a paragraph. And the parser does not report the error — it repairs it. The moment it meets
inside an open

, it closes the paragraph immediately, leaving the div outside it and often a stray empty paragraph behind. That silent repair means your page can render 'mostly fine' while its real structure differs from your source — until a CSS rule targets p and mysteriously misses half the text. The fix is always the same: if the content is inline, use an inline wrapper (span); if it is genuinely a block, move it out of the paragraph.

Friday

sections.heading: Display is ultimately CSS's decision
sections.body:
Everything above describes defaults and validity — what HTML allows and how elements render before any styling. CSS then has the final word on presentation: display: block makes a link stack like a paragraph, display: inline-block gives a span dimensions, display: flex and grid turn a div into a layout engine for its children.

What CSS cannot change is validity. Setting display: inline on a div does not make it legal inside a span or a p — the parser repaired the tree long before CSS ran. Write markup that is valid by HTML's rules, then restyle its rendering as freely as the design demands.

This boundary — structure decided in HTML, presentation decided in CSS — is the theme of the next lessons, where CSS enters the course properly.

lessons.whyItMatters: class and id are the naming system of the web: CSS rules, JavaScript lookups and fragment links all find elements through them. Choose names well and a stylesheet reads like documentation; choose badly and every change becomes a hunt. Nearly every line of CSS you will ever write starts by referencing a class, so learning to apply them cleanly now pays off for the rest of the course.

The id is different: signup appears exactly once in the document, which is what lets the fragment link scroll to it and lets JavaScript's getElementById find it without ambiguity. Classes answer 'what kind of thing is this?'; ids answer 'which exact thing is this?'.
lessons.example:

With class="note" on all three asides, one CSS rule styles them identically; adding important to one of them layers a second style on top. With id="signup" on the form's heading, the page gains a shareable deep link and a JavaScript handle in one attribute.

commonMistakes: Reusing an id on two elements. Ids must be unique per page: duplicates break fragment links, JavaScript lookups and label associations in quiet, confusing ways.
Writing class="note" class="important" as two attributes. An element takes one class attribute; multiple names go inside it separated by spaces.
Naming classes after their looks (red-text, big-box). The first redesign makes the names lies; name the role instead (note, warning, price).
Putting spaces in id values. An id must be a single token — spaces split it into nonsense and the CSS selector #my id will never match.
lessons.proTip: A practical convention used across the industry: lowercase names with hyphens (signup-form, note-important), classes for anything CSS styles, and ids reserved for fragment targets and form label wiring. Some teams go as far as never styling ids at all — their high specificity makes CSS harder to override later.

coding.intro: You will give a newsletter page the labels that CSS, links and JavaScript rely on: reusable classes, a stacked pair of classes, and one unique id.

sections.heading: class: reusable labels for kinds of things
sections.body:
The class attribute attaches one or more names to an element. The names mean nothing to the browser by themselves — no styling changes, no behavior — but they create hooks: CSS selects by class to style every matching element at once, and JavaScript queries by class to operate on the whole set.

Any element can carry a class, and — this is the point — many elements can carry the same one. Mark every informational aside on a site with class="note" and a single CSS rule styles all of them, today and every note you add next year. The class is a statement: 'this element is one of these'.

The attribute is written once per element: class="note". Its value is your choice entirely; HTML predefines no class names.

sections.heading: Multiple classes on one element
sections.body:
One class attribute can hold several names, separated by spaces: class="note important" makes the element a member of both the note group and the important group. It inherits every rule written for either class, with the normal CSS cascade resolving any conflicts.

This is how styling stays composable. The base class carries the shared look (every note gets the same background and padding); modifier classes layer variations on top (important adds a stronger border). Rather than inventing note-red, note-big, note-red-big for every combination, you combine small single-purpose classes.

Order inside the attribute does not matter — class="important note" is identical — and duplicate names are ignored. What does matter is the space: it is the separator, which is exactly why an individual class name can never contain one.

sections.heading: id: one name, one element
sections.body:
The id attribute gives an element a name that must be unique on the page. Where class says 'one of these', id says 'the one'. That uniqueness is a real contract, not a style preference: three separate mechanisms depend on it.

Fragment links scroll to ids — href="#signup" finds the element with id="signup", as you saw in the links lesson. JavaScript's fastest lookup, document.getElementById('signup'), returns the one element (and silently returns only the first if you break the contract with duplicates). And form labels bind to inputs by id, which is what makes clicking a label focus its field.

An id value must contain no spaces, and in practice you should keep it to letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter. It is case-sensitive: Signup and signup are different names — one more reason to stay lowercase everywhere.

Sign up

Go to signup

sections.heading: Choosing between class and id
sections.body:
The decision rule is short: could there ever be a second one? Notes, cards, buttons, warnings — of course there could; those are classes. The page's single signup section, the site header, the main content region — one per page by definition; those may take ids.

When in doubt, choose class. A class used once costs nothing and is ready if a second instance appears. An id that turns out to need a sibling forces renaming and breaks whatever pointed at it. Many experienced developers style exclusively with classes and reserve ids for the jobs only ids can do: fragment targets, getElementById, and form label wiring.

The two attributes coexist happily on one element: <section id="signup" class="panel"> is a common shape — unique identity for linking, shared class for styling.

sections.heading: Naming that survives redesigns
sections.body:
Names are for the humans who maintain the page, so optimize them for meaning. Name what the element is, not what it currently looks like: class="warning" outlives class="red-text" the day warnings turn orange. Keep names lowercase and hyphen-separated (reader-note, signup-form) — the style used by virtually every CSS codebase.

Consistency beats cleverness. A page where every label follows one convention can be skimmed like a table of contents; a page mixing warningBox, Warning_2 and redtext must be deciphered. Larger projects formalize this with naming systems (you may meet BEM, with names like card__title--large), but the underlying discipline is the same one you are practicing here.

A last habit worth stealing: before adding a new class, check whether an existing one already means the same thing. Vocabulary that stays small stays learnable.

sections.heading: How CSS and JavaScript consume these labels
sections.body:
You will meet CSS properly in the next lesson, but the selector syntax belongs here because it mirrors the attributes exactly. In a stylesheet, .note (leading dot) selects every element whose class list contains note; #signup (leading hash) selects the element with that id; .note.important — two selectors glued together — matches only elements carrying both classes.

JavaScript reads the same names: document.getElementById('signup') for ids (no hash — the method name already says id), and document.querySelectorAll('.note') to collect every note using CSS selector syntax. The names you put in your HTML today are the exact strings those tools will match tomorrow.

This is why tidy labeling is not cosmetic. Every selector, every script, every deep link is a promise that a name exists in the markup — and you are writing those names now.

lessons.title: Give HTML its looks: inline styles, style blocks and stylesheets
lessons.summary: Meet CSS at the HTML boundary: the style attribute, the style element in the head, external stylesheets via link, and how the three layers cascade.
lessons.goal: Style a tea shop page three ways — one inline style, a style block with body and h1 rules, and a linked external stylesheet.
lessons.whyItMatters: Every real page pairs HTML with CSS, and where you attach the CSS shapes the whole project: inline styles are quick and unmaintainable, style blocks suit single pages, and external stylesheets are how every production site shares one design across hundreds of pages. Understanding the three attachment points — and which wins when they disagree — is the foundation for all the styling you will ever do.
steps: Read the section on the HTML/CSS boundary.

lessons.explanation: Three attachment points appear here. The style attribute paints one element directly — fastest to write, hardest to maintain. The style element holds real CSS rules that apply across this one page: each rule is a selector (body, h1) plus declarations of property: value pairs. The link element pulls in a shared stylesheet file that any number of pages can reuse; it is a void element in the head, just like the favicon link.
lessons.example:

After this lesson the body carries a warm background and a chosen typeface, the h1 sits centered in the shop's green, the promo line pops in dark red — and a stylesheet link stands ready so tomorrow's second page can inherit the same design from one shared file.

commonMistakes: Writing CSS syntax in HTML attributes or vice versa. Inside style="..." and style blocks it is property: value with colons and semicolons — not the equals sign HTML attributes use.
Placing the style element in the body. It belongs in the head; browsers tolerate it elsewhere, but you invite a flash of unstyled content and validation errors.
Writing <link rel="stylesheet"> but forgetting the href — or closing link with </link>. It is a void element and needs both rel and href to do anything.
Reaching for inline styles as the default. Ten paragraphs styled inline are ten places to edit; one class-based rule is one.
lessons.proTip: You can watch the cascade argue in DevTools: inspect any element and the Styles panel lists every rule that targets it, with the losers shown crossed out. It is the fastest way to answer 'why is this text still black?' — usually a more specific or later rule is winning.

coding.intro: You will style one page three different ways — inline, in a head style block, and via a linked stylesheet — and see why real projects prefer the third.

sections.heading: Where HTML stops and CSS begins
sections.body:
HTML answers one question: what is this content? A heading, a list, a link. CSS answers a different one: how should it look? Color, size, spacing, alignment, typeface. The two languages are deliberately separate, and the separation is the single most important design decision in web platform history: content survives redesigns, one stylesheet can reskin a thousand pages, and machines reading your HTML are never misled by decoration.

CSS is written as declarations — property: value pairs like color: darkred — grouped into rules that say which elements they apply to. HTML's role is only to host or reference that CSS, and it offers exactly three attachment points: an attribute on one element, a style element in the page, and a link to a separate file. This lesson walks through all three.

A small vocabulary note before the syntax: in color: darkred, the property is color, the value is darkred, and the colon binds them. Semicolons separate multiple declarations. Getting colons and semicolons swapped is the classic first-day CSS typo.

sections.heading: The style attribute: inline styles
sections.body:
Any visible element accepts a style attribute whose value is a list of CSS declarations applied to that element only:

. No selector is needed — the attribute already sits on its target. Inline styles are immediate and precise, which is exactly their problem. The styling lives inside the content, so changing a design means hunting through markup; nothing is reusable, so the same declaration gets pasted onto every similar element; and inline declarations override nearly everything else, making later stylesheets fight to take effect. They also cannot express hover effects, media queries, or anything beyond plain declarations. Legitimate uses survive: quick experiments, HTML email (where support for anything else is poor), and values computed by JavaScript at runtime. For everything else, treat the style attribute as the exception you can read, not the tool you reach for.
sections.code: Today only: free shipping.

sections.heading: The style element: page-level CSS
sections.body:
The second attachment point is a style element in the head. Everything inside it is genuine CSS: rules made of a selector, braces, and declarations. body { background-color: #f4efe6; } paints the whole page's background; h1 { text-align: center; } centers every h1 on the page.

The selectors are the same vocabulary you met in the classes lesson: element names select every instance of a tag, .note selects by class, #signup selects by id. One rule, many elements — this is the reuse inline styles cannot offer, and it is why even a single-page project should prefer a style block over scattered style attributes.

The style element's scope is the one page containing it. That makes it right for one-off pages, demos and email templates — and wrong for a multi-page site, where the same block would be copied into every page and drift out of sync.
sections.code:
<head>
  <style>
    body { background-color: #f4efe6; font-family: Georgia, serif; }
    h1   { text-align: center; color: #3b5d50; }
  </style>
</head>

sections.heading: link rel="stylesheet": one file, every page
sections.body:
The third attachment point moves the CSS out of the HTML entirely: a .css file containing only rules, referenced from the head with <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">. The link element is void — no closing tag — and its two attributes do all the work: rel declares the relationship (this file is a stylesheet for me) and href locates the file.

This is how essentially every production site works, because the benefits compound: one file styles unlimited pages, so a redesign edits one place; browsers cache the file, so every page after the first loads faster; and content people can edit HTML while design people edit CSS without touching each other's files.

A page may link several stylesheets, and links can sit alongside a style block. In this exercise the linked file does not actually exist — the link is still valid markup, and in a real project it would be the first file you create.
sections.code:
<head>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">
</head>

sections.heading: When the layers disagree: the cascade
sections.body:
With three attachment points, conflicts are inevitable — the stylesheet says the paragraph is black, the style block says green, the inline style says dark red. CSS resolves this with the cascade, and for now one paragraph of it is enough: more specific beats less specific (an id rule beats a class rule beats a plain element rule), inline style attributes beat all three, and when two rules are otherwise equal, the one declared later wins — so a style block after the link overrides the linked file, and the last rule in a sheet overrides an identical earlier one. Browser defaults sit at the bottom of the pile, which is why your rules always take effect over them.

That ordering explains the standard head convention: link elements first, page-specific style blocks after, so page tweaks can override the shared design. It also explains the deeper reason inline styles are avoided: sitting at the top of the cascade, they can only be beaten by heavy machinery, which turns stylesheets into arms races.

sections.heading: Five properties to make pages visibly yours
sections.body:
The rest of CSS belongs to its own course; these five properties are enough to make every exercise from here on visual. color sets text color, and background-color paints the area behind an element — set both deliberately so text stays readable. font-family chooses the typeface, written as a wish list ending in a generic fallback: Georgia, serif asks for Georgia and accepts any serif if it is missing.

font-size sets text size (16px is the browser's default paragraph size; units get their own lesson in the CSS course). text-align aligns text within its block — left, center, right or justify — and is the honest way to center a heading.

Everything you learned about labeling now pays off: these properties become powerful when aimed through selectors at the classes and ids you already know how to write.

body { background-color: #f4efe6; color: #222222; }
h1   { font-family: Georgia, serif; font-size: 40px; text-align: center; }

lessons.title: Speak color fluently: names, hex, rgb() and hsl()
lessons.summary: Write the same color four ways — keywords, hex codes, rgb()/rgba() and hsl()/hsla() — and keep text readable with real contrast.
lessons.goal: Fill a brand-palette tester with one swatch per color notation and give the hero banner a dark background with properly contrasting light text.
lessons.whyItMatters: Colors appear in every design conversation, and each notation exists for a reason: names for quick drafts, hex because every design tool exports it, rgb() and hsl() when you need transparency or systematic palette adjustments. Reading all four fluently means you can use any designer's handoff, any brand guide, any code you inherit — and contrast literacy keeps what you build legible and accessible.
steps: Read how color notations relate to each other.
Paint the first swatch with a named color (task 1).

Read the contrast section, then give the hero a dark background with white text (task 5).

lessons.explanation: Four notations, one idea: telling the screen how much red, green and blue to emit. The keyword teal is a fixed shade from a predefined list; #2e6f6c states the three channels in hexadecimal; rgb(46, 111, 108) states them in decimal; hsl(177, 41%, 31%) describes the same color as a hue angle, saturation and lightness — the version humans can reason about. The final pair shows the discipline that matters most: background and text color chosen together so the text stays readable.
lessons.example:
A brand guide arrives saying the primary color is #2e6f6c. The junior developer who only knows color names is stuck; the one who reads hex recognizes a muted teal, converts it to hsl(177, 41%, 31%) to derive lighter and darker variants by adjusting the last number, and uses rgba(46, 111, 108, 0.15) for a translucent tint of the same brand color.

Same color, four notations, each earning its place in one workflow.

commonMistakes: Dropping the # from hex codes. background-color: 2e6f6c is invalid and silently ignored — the page just stays unstyled.
Setting a text color with no thought for what is behind it (or vice versa). The pair is one decision; grey on grey is the classic accident.
Writing rgb percentages and numbers inconsistently or forgetting the % on hsl saturation and lightness — hsl(177, 41, 31) does nothing.
Trusting color names beyond the basics. darkgray is famously lighter than gray; past the common dozen names, check rather than guess.
lessons.proTip: Every browser's DevTools includes a contrast checker: inspect a text element, click the small color swatch in the Styles panel, and it reports the contrast ratio against the background with pass/fail marks for the WCAG targets (4.5:1 for body text). Make checking it a reflex whenever you pick a text/background pair.

coding.intro: You will paint the same brand teal in four notations and build one high-contrast banner — the complete color toolkit for HTML and CSS work.

sections.heading: One color, many spellings
sections.body:
Screens make color by mixing three channels of light — red, green and blue — each dialed from 0 to 255. Every CSS color notation is just a different way of writing those three dials (sometimes plus a fourth for transparency), which means the notations are fully interchangeable: teal, #008080, rgb(0, 128, 128) and hsl(180, 100%, 25%) are the identical pixel.

Colors go wherever CSS goes — inline style attributes, style blocks, stylesheets — through properties like color (the text) and background-color (the area behind it). In this lesson you will write them into style attributes so each swatch shows its result immediately.

Why learn four spellings of the same thing? Because each dominates a different context: names in teaching and quick tests, hex in design handoffs, rgb() in image-editor exports and transparency work, hsl() wherever palettes are built systematically. Fluency means never being stopped by the notation a project happens to use.

sections.heading: Named colors: the quick draft
sections.body:
CSS predefines around 140 color keywords. A handful you will use forever: black, white, red, green, blue, gray, orange, purple, teal, navy, plus the honorary member transparent. The rest range from tomato and gold to curiosities like papayawhip — real, but rarely seen in production.

Names are unbeatable for speed: background-color: teal needs no lookup and no tooling. Their weakness is precision — no brand's palette happens to match a keyword, and some names mislead (darkgray is lighter than gray, a genuine historical accident of the list). So names serve drafts, examples and tests, and then hex or hsl takes over.

Names are case-insensitive; the lowercase convention is universal.
sections.code: Named: teal

sections.heading: Hex codes: the industry's exchange format
sections.body:
A hex code is a # followed by six hexadecimal digits — two per channel, in red-green-blue order. Hexadecimal counts 0-9 then a-f, so each pair runs from 00 (channel off) to ff (channel fully on): #ff0000 is pure red, #000000 black, #ffffff white, #2e6f6c a muted teal. Letter case does not matter.

A three-digit shorthand exists for codes whose pairs are doubled digits: #fff expands to #ffffff, #c30 to #cc3300. You will see the short form constantly in handwritten CSS. An eight-digit form (#2e6f6c80) appends a fourth pair for transparency, though rgba/hsla are more common for that.

Hex is the lingua franca: Figma, Photoshop and every color picker export it, and brand guides are written in it. You do not need to compute hex in your head — you need to recognize the shape, spot roughly what it says (high red pair, low blue pair: warm color), and paste it accurately, never forgetting the #.
sections.code: Hex: #2e6f6c

sections.heading: rgb() and rgba(): decimal channels and transparency
sections.body:
The rgb() function states the three channels in ordinary decimal, 0 to 255: rgb(46, 111, 108) is the same muted teal as #2e6f6c. Nothing hex says is beyond rgb() — it is the same numbers in a base humans read natively, which is why image editors report colors this way.

Its historic superpower is the fourth channel: rgba() adds alpha, opacity from 0 (invisible) to 1 (solid). rgba(46, 111, 108, 0.5) is the teal at half transparency — the tool behind tinted overlays on photos, soft shadows, and translucent panels. Alpha differs from lightening a color: a half-transparent teal lets whatever is behind it show through, while a paler teal is just a different solid color.

Modern CSS also accepts a slash syntax — rgb(46 111 108 / 0.5) — and treats rgb()/rgba() as one function. The comma forms remain fully valid and are what you will meet most in existing code.
sections.code:
RGB

Half-transparent overlay

sections.heading: hsl() and hsla(): color the way people think
sections.body:
hsl() abandons channel arithmetic for three human questions. Hue: which direction on the color wheel, in degrees — 0 red, 120 green, 240 blue, wrapping back to red at 360. Saturation: how vivid, 0% (gray) to 100% (pure). Lightness: how bright, 0% (black) through 50% (the pure color) to 100% (white). The brand teal becomes hsl(177, 41%, 31%): a cyan-ish hue, moderately muted, on the dark side.

The payoff is systematic palettes. Need a hover shade? Same hue and saturation, nudge the lightness: hsl(177, 41%, 41%). Need a whole scale from pale tint to deep shade? Hold hue, walk lightness from 90% down to 15%. Doing that in hex means recalculating three channels; in hsl it is editing one number. hsla() (or the slash syntax) adds the same alpha channel as rgba().

Both percent signs are mandatory — hsl(177, 41, 31) is invalid and silently ignored, one of the easiest color bugs to write.
sections.code: HSL

sections.heading: Contrast: the pair is the decision
sections.body:
Text color and background color are not two choices but one: what matters is the difference between them. That difference is measured as a contrast ratio from 1:1 (identical) to 21:1 (black on white), and the WCAG accessibility guidelines set the working targets — at least 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large headings. These are not bureaucratic niceties: low-contrast text is what makes pages unreadable on a sunlit phone screen or with aging eyes.

The reliable recipe is dark-on-light or light-on-dark, committed to fully. A near-black background like #1a1a2e with white text lands around 16:1 — effortless reading. The failures are always the timid middles: mid-gray on light gray, white on yellow, brand-color text on a tinted background of the same brand color.

Two habits complete the discipline. Whenever you set a background-color, set color in the same rule (and vice versa) so you never inherit an unreadable combination by accident. And verify rather than eyeball — DevTools' built-in contrast checker gives you the ratio in one click.

A well-formed head is the difference between a page that merely renders and one that presents itself properly to browsers, search engines and social platforms.

The viewport meta tells phones to render at their real screen width instead of pretending to be desktops. The title feeds the tab, bookmarks and search results; the description meta feeds the snippet below the search result; and the author meta credits the maker. None of this renders in the page itself — the head is metadata, information about the document rather than content of it.

Stuffing the description with keywords. It is your search-result ad copy — one clear sentence outperforms a comma-salad, and Google rewrites bad ones anyway.

coding.intro: You will assemble a production-quality head, line by line, and learn what each piece of metadata does for browsers, phones and search engines.

sections.heading: The document's control panel
sections.body:
An HTML document splits into two halves with opposite jobs. The body holds everything a visitor sees. The head holds information about the document — its title, its character encoding, its relationship to other files, instructions for phones and search engines. Nothing placed in the head renders on the page.

That invisibility misleads beginners into treating the head as boilerplate to paste and forget. In reality every line answers a question some system will ask: What do I put on the tab? (title). How do I decode these bytes? (charset). How wide should I render on this phone? (viewport). What snippet represents this page in results? (description). Which stylesheet applies? (link).

The head is written between <head> and </head>, before the body. You have already been placing title, style and link elements there; this lesson completes the set with the meta family.
sections.code:
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <!-- metadata: about the page -->
</head>
<body>
  <!-- content: the page -->
</body>
</html>

sections.heading: title: the page's public name
sections.body:
The title element sets the document's name — required in every valid HTML document, exactly one per page, plain text only. Its reach is wider than the tab: it labels bookmarks, appears in the browser history, is announced first by screen readers when a page loads, and becomes the blue headline of your search result. Search engines also treat its words as a strong relevance signal, which makes it one of the highest-leverage lines of SEO you control.

Good titles are specific and front-loaded: the page's own subject first, the site name after a separator — 'Sourdough Loaves — Crumb & Crust' rather than 'Crumb & Crust | Products | Page 2'. Keep it under roughly 60 characters so results do not truncate it, and give every page of a site a distinct title; twelve tabs all reading 'Home' help no one.

Do not confuse title with the h1. The h1 is content, visible in the page; the title is metadata, visible everywhere else. They often carry similar text, and that is fine — they are still two different elements doing two different jobs.
sections.code: <title>Crumb & Crust — Neighbourhood Bakery</title>

sections.heading: The meta element and charset
sections.body:
meta is the head's general-purpose metadata carrier: a void element whose attributes hold the data. It comes in two main shapes. The first is the special one-attribute form <meta charset="UTF-8">, which declares the character encoding — the rulebook translating the file's raw bytes back into letters. Declare UTF-8 always; it encodes every character of every language, and the next lesson explores what goes wrong without it.

Position matters for this one meta: the browser needs the encoding before it can safely read anything else, so the declaration must sit within the first 1024 bytes of the file. The universal convention is to make it the first line inside the head, and there is no reason to deviate.

The second shape is the name/content pair — <meta name="..." content="..."> — a small key-value store for everything else: description, author, viewport and more. The name says which property, the content carries its value.
sections.code:
<meta charset="UTF-8">
<meta name="author" content="Crumb & Crust">

sections.heading: description and author
sections.body:
The description meta is your page's one-sentence pitch: <meta name="description" content="Sourdough, rye and pastries baked before sunrise...">. Search engines display it as the gray snippet under your result — it does not affect ranking, but it heavily affects whether people click. Write it like ad copy: one or two natural sentences, roughly 150-160 characters, unique per page. Leave it out and search engines improvise a snippet from whatever page text matched the query, with mixed results.

The author meta simply credits a person or organization: <meta name="author" content="N. Kim">. Tools and archives read it; search engines largely ignore it. It costs one line and documents provenance.

One meta you will see in old code and should never write: name="keywords". It was abused into meaninglessness decades ago, and every major search engine ignores it completely.

sections.heading: viewport: the line that makes pages mobile
sections.body:
When smartphones first got real browsers, the web was desktop-only — so phone browsers lied: they rendered pages onto an imaginary desktop-width canvas (about 980px) and zoomed out to fit the screen. Legacy pages survived as tiny-but-complete miniatures; users pinch-zoomed around them. Phone browsers still do this today for any page that does not say otherwise.

The viewport meta is how you say otherwise: <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">. width=device-width sets the layout canvas to the phone's true screen width; initial-scale=1.0 starts at 100% zoom. With it, your text renders at readable size and your CSS can respond to the real screen; without it, no amount of styling makes a page genuinely mobile-friendly, and Google flags the page in its mobile checks.

This line is non-negotiable boilerplate for every page you will ever ship. Resist the old temptation to bolt on user-scalable=no to stop pinch-zooming — zoom is an accessibility feature, and disabling it locks out low-vision users.
sections.code: <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">

sections.heading: base, and the ordering conventions
sections.body:
One rarer head element completes the inventory: base sets the starting point for every relative URL in the document. <base href="https://example.com/docs/"> makes a link to guide.html resolve inside /docs/; <base target="_blank"> makes every link default to a new tab. At most one base is allowed, it must precede any element that uses URLs, and it is a blunt instrument — it rewrites all relative links at once — so most sites simply never use it. Recognize it; reach for it rarely.

A conventional head reads in this order: charset first (the decoding rule), viewport next (the rendering rule), then title, then the remaining metas, then link elements for stylesheets and icons, then any style block. The order is mostly convention rather than law, but conventions shared by millions of developers are worth keeping — anyone can skim your head and find what they expect where they expect it.

Finally, placement of scripts: script elements may live in the head or the body, but a script in the head blocks page rendering while it loads. The long-standing pattern is stylesheets in the head (so the page never renders unstyled) and scripts at the end of the body — or in the head with the defer attribute, which tells the browser to keep rendering and run the script after the document is parsed.

Both bugs come from the same two systems: character encoding, which maps bytes to characters, and entities, which let you write characters HTML would otherwise misread. Master the small required set and the common symbols, and text handling stops being a source of mystery bugs.
