sections.heading: Bytes, characters, and why pages garble
sections.body:
A file on disk is only bytes — numbers. A character encoding is the agreed table that maps those numbers back to letters: 72 means H, and so on. The old encodings (ASCII, then regional ones like Latin-1 or ISO-8859-7 for Greek) each covered one alphabet in 256 slots, which is why the early web garbled anything that crossed a language boundary.

UTF-8 ended that era: one encoding that represents every character in Unicode — every alphabet, every symbol, every emoji — while staying byte-compatible with ASCII for plain English text. It is the encoding of effectively the entire modern web, and there is no reason to author in anything else.

The garbling you have seen — â‚¬ where € should be, Ã© instead of é — is what happens when text saved under one encoding is decoded under another. The bytes are fine; the reader used the wrong table. Which raises the question: how does a browser know which table to use?

sections.heading: meta charset: pinning the decoding
sections.body:
The browser learns the encoding from your declaration: <meta charset="UTF-8"> in the head. It must appear early — within the first 1024 bytes — because the browser is already decoding as it reads; convention puts it as the first line inside head. Without a declaration the browser guesses from the bytes, and guesses are exactly what work on your machine and fail on someone else's.

Two halves make the system work, and they must agree: your editor saves the file as UTF-8 (every modern editor's default), and your meta declares UTF-8. The declaration does not convert anything — it describes. Declaring UTF-8 on a file actually saved as Latin-1 garbles it just as surely as declaring nothing.

With both halves in place, you can type ©, €, ü, Ω or 🎉 directly into your HTML and they render perfectly. That is the modern baseline — and it makes entities a targeted tool rather than a constant chore.
sections.code:
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <title>The Markup Cafe</title>
</head>

sections.heading: Entities: writing characters by name
sections.body:
An entity is a way to write one character as a short code: an ampersand, a name (or a # plus a number), and a closing semicolon. < produces <. © and © both produce ©. The browser replaces the code with the character when rendering; your source shows the code, your visitors see the symbol.

Why would anyone write characters indirectly? Two reasons. First: some characters ARE HTML syntax — type a literal < and the parser starts reading a tag. Entities let you display those characters instead of triggering them. Second, historically: characters you could not type or save reliably. UTF-8 has mostly retired the second reason, but the first is permanent.

All three parts are mandatory. Omit the semicolon and you are writing invalid HTML that happens to render sometimes; names are case-sensitive (© is not a thing). When an entity seems to 'not work', check those two details first.

&  →  &
" →  "
© →  ©
€ → € (numeric form; € also works)

sections.heading: The required escapes: < > and &
sections.body: Three characters have non-negotiable escaping rules because they carry syntax meaning. The less-than sign must be written < whenever you want it displayed as text — a literal < in prose makes the parser open a phantom tag and can swallow everything up to the next >. Writing about HTML in HTML, as this course constantly does, means <p> every time a tag name appears as content. The greater-than sign is safer in practice, but the rule of the pair is: escape both, always, and never think about edge cases. The ampersand is subtler: & is the character that BEGINS entities, so a bare one is ambiguous — is 'Fish & Chips' text, or the start of &Chi...? Browsers usually recover, but validators flag it and edge cases bite. Write & wherever an ampersand is content, including inside attribute values: a URL with parameters becomes href="search?a=1&b=2". The quote entities " (") and ' (') are required only in one situation: inside an attribute value delimited by the same quote character. — otherwise the inner quotes would end the attribute early. In ordinary text, quotes need no escaping at all.

sections.heading: and the useful symbol set
sections.body:
is the non-breaking space: it renders like a normal space but forbids the browser from wrapping a line at it. Use it to glue pairs that must not separate — 10 GB, 25 °C, page 7 — so a line break never strands the unit from its number. What it is NOT for is layout: chains of     to indent or space things out is a relic of the 1990s; spacing belongs to CSS. Note also that consecutive normal spaces collapse into one when rendered — another reason people once abused   — but the correct response is CSS, not entity chains.

A small symbol vocabulary covers most real needs: © ©, ® ®, ™ ™, € €, £ £, ¥ ¥, ° °, × ×, ÷ ÷, — — (the long dash), … …, and the arrows ← ↑ → ↓. Every one also has a numeric form (© equals ©), which exists for the thousands of characters without names.

And emoji? Just characters. With UTF-8 declared, paste 🎉 directly — no entity needed, though 🎉 would produce the same party popper. Emoji in HTML need no special treatment whatsoever; that is the whole point of a universal encoding.

sections.heading: A related system: URL encoding
sections.body:
You will meet a second escaping system living right next to this one: URLs have their own reserved characters and their own escape syntax, percent-encoding. A space cannot appear in a URL, so it becomes %20 — a percent sign plus the character's byte value in hexadecimal. my file.pdf is fetched as my%20file.pdf; non-ASCII characters encode as multi-byte sequences, which is why a Greek word in a URL balloons into %CE%B1-style runs.

Browsers largely handle this for you: type a space or paste ω into the address bar or click such an href, and the browser encodes on the wire while showing you the readable form. You mostly notice percent-encoding when copying URLs out of the address bar or when building URLs in code.

Keep the two systems distinct in your head: entities (&) escape characters for HTML's parser; percent-codes (%20) escape characters for URLs. They never substitute for each other — and the one place they meet is the one you already know: a URL used inside an href still writes its parameter-joining ampersands as &, because the attribute value is HTML first.

coding.intro: No new elements — just you, an almost-empty file, and everything the course has taught, assembled into a page worth keeping.

sections.heading: Plan before you type
sections.body:
Professionals do not start pages by typing tags; they start by deciding the outline. For a profile page the questions take one minute: What is the single h1? (Your name.) What are the major sections? (About, Skills, Contact — three h2s.) What does each section contain? (A paragraph and a photo; a list; two links.) Write that down, even as a comment, and the rest of the build is filling in blanks.

The payoff of planning is that every later decision becomes local. When you add the photo you are only asking 'what belongs in About?', not 'what is my page?'. When structure questions and content questions are answered separately, neither gets rushed.

This lesson's tasks follow that exact order deliberately: skeleton first, structure second, content third, finishing touches last. It is the order to internalize for every page you build after this one.

sections.heading: The skeleton, from memory this time
sections.body:
Every valid page stands on the same five-line frame, and by now you should be able to write it without reference: the doctype declaration first — <!DOCTYPE html>, above everything, telling the browser to use modern standards rendering — then the html element with its lang attribute, containing exactly two children: head and body.

The head carries the metadata set you assembled in lesson 22: meta charset first, the viewport meta, and a title that will label the tab and the search result. For a profile page, make the title your name plus a word of context — 'Alex Petrou — Student Developer' — since 'My page' helps no search engine and no bookmark list.

One detail this exercise makes you handle: the starter file is missing its doctype. A page without one still renders, but in quirks mode — the browser's bug-compatibility emulation of the 1990s — with subtly wrong layout behavior. First task, one line, permanent habit.

sections.heading: Headings make the outline real
sections.body:
Your plan becomes markup through the heading rules of lesson 6: exactly one h1 — your name, since the whole page is about you — and one h2 per major section: About, Skills, Contact. No levels skipped; subsections, if you ever add them, become h3s under their h2.

Read the finished outline as a table of contents to check it: Alex Petrou — About — Skills — Contact. Sensible. That reading is exactly what a screen-reader user does with a headings shortcut, and roughly what a search engine extracts, so if the outline reads well, the page's bones are right.

Resist the decorative temptation one more time: if a section title should look smaller, that will be a CSS decision in the next course. Levels encode structure, not size — the discipline you have practiced since the headings lesson.

sections.heading: Body text, formatting and the photo
sections.body:
The About section wants two or three honest sentences, in real p elements, with inline formatting doing semantic work: strong for what genuinely matters ('currently seeking an internship'), em for stress ('I enjoy the debugging most'), never bold-as-decoration. One well-formatted paragraph outperforms five plain ones.

The photo applies lesson 14 end to end: src naming the file, width and height so the layout never jumps, and alt text describing the image for whoever cannot see it — 'Alex smiling in front of a whiteboard', not 'photo' and not empty, because a portrait on a profile page is content, not decoration.

The Skills section applies lesson 16: enumerable items are a ul of li elements, one skill per item, no comma-lists inside a paragraph. Order does not rank you, so unordered is the honest choice — and when you later learn CSS grid, this same list restyles into a tag cloud without touching the markup.

sections.heading: Contact links, done safely
sections.body:
The Contact section replays lesson 13 with real stakes, because these are links you will actually publish. The external link — your GitHub, portfolio, or a professional profile — opens in a new tab so visitors keep your page: target="_blank", always paired with rel="noopener" so the destination gets no scripting handle on your page.

The email link uses the mailto: scheme, address glued directly to the colon. Show the address (or a clear label) as the link text, remembering that visitors without a configured mail client will want to copy it. If you add a phone number, tel: with the international +30-style prefix is the pattern.

Small real-world note: publishing an email address in a public page does attract scrapers and spam. For a learning page with an example.com address it is a non-issue; for your real site you might prefer a contact form later — a topic for the forms lesson.

sections.heading: Finishing touches: entity, comment, audit
sections.body:
Two small finishers separate a complete page from an abandoned draft. The footer line — © year and your name — writes its copyright symbol as the entity ©, applying lesson 23. And a source comment records what the page needs next: <!-- last updated Aug 2026; add project links next -->. Comments render nowhere; they exist for the maintainer, who in six months will be you with no memory of today.
